blocks.text: Give clients a uniform way to walk a collection's elements without exposing how it stores them.

The **aggregate** hands out an **iterator**, a small cursor object that knows the traversal state: where it is and what comes next. Clients depend only on `hasNext` and `next`, so a list, a tree or a lazy generator all look the same, and several traversals can run at once.

items: **Hides:** the internal structure (array, tree, linked nodes, database cursor).
**Holds:** the traversal position, separate from the collection.
**Enables:** several independent, lazy traversals over one aggregate.

blocks.text: In Java, implementing `Iterable<T>` is what makes a type usable in the enhanced `for` loop.

walkthrough.note: The aggregate is a binary search tree. Its node type and links are private: callers can add elements but never see the structure.
`iterator()` returns a fresh cursor each call. The cursor keeps an explicit stack of pending nodes, so traversal state lives in the iterator, not in the tree.
Because the tree implements `Iterable`, the enhanced `for` works. The client sees elements in sorted order and has no idea a tree exists.
Iteration is lazy: only the nodes needed so far are visited. A second iterator would have its own stack and be independent.

blocks.text: Streaming a large database table to a CSV export.

A reporting job must export millions of orders without loading them into memory. A repository returns an iterator that fetches a page at a time through a server-side cursor, hiding the paging and the connection handling. The exporter loops over `orders` and writes rows. Closing the iterator releases the cursor, so it implements `AutoCloseable` as well.
Payoff: constant memory for any table size, and the exporter works unchanged against an in-memory fake in tests.

lists.title: Use when
items: Callers should traverse without depending on the storage structure.
You need several simultaneous or lazy traversals of one collection.
Different traversal orders (in-order, level-order) share one interface.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: A plain list or array is enough and random access is needed.
Operations such as map and filter are the real goal: use streams.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Modifying the collection during traversal: JDK iterators are fail-fast and throw `ConcurrentModificationException`.
Iterators that hold resources (cursors, files) and are never closed.
Assuming `Iterator` instances are thread-safe; they are not.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: `Iterable` powers the `for-each` loop; `Stream` and `spliterator()` cover bulk and parallel pipelines.
Most code writes `for` or streams; you hand-write an `Iterator` only for your own data structures.

rows.difference: Iterators are the usual way to traverse a composite tree without exposing its node structure to clients.
An iterator hands out elements and the client decides what to do. A visitor pushes an operation into the elements and picks behavior per element type.
An iterator can use a memento to save and restore its position, for example to rewind or resume a scan.
`iterator()` is a factory method: each aggregate subclass decides which concrete iterator to create.
An iterator is pulled by the client, one element at a time. An observer is pushed to by the subject whenever something happens.

options.why: A separate cursor holds the position and exposes sequential access while the array stays hidden.
There is no tree of parts and wholes, only a flat sequence being walked.
Nothing captures state for later restoration; the index only advances.
Elements are pulled by the client; nothing is pushed to registered listeners.

exercises.scenario: A metrics library stores samples in a ring buffer to avoid allocations. Callers must read samples oldest to newest without knowing about wrap-around, and a dashboard thread may read while another one also reads.

options.why: Each reader gets its own cursor that hides the ring layout and tracks its own position.
Samples are one type; there is no need to dispatch per element type, only sequential access.
Nobody needs to restore earlier buffer states; the need is ordered traversal.
No group of objects needs coordinating; one structure needs a traversal API.

exercises.prompt: Explain Iterator in your own words: what it hides, where the traversal state lives, and why that matters.

modelAnswer.text: Iterator gives clients sequential access to an aggregate without revealing its structure. The traversal state lives in a separate cursor object, not the collection, so several traversals can run independently and lazily. In Java, Iterable plus the for-each loop is the idiom.

keyPoints: Hides the internal structure of the aggregate
Traversal state lives in the iterator, not the collection
Multiple independent, lazy traversals are possible
Concurrent modification needs a policy such as fail-fast
